evidences.title: Hurricane Sandy one year on: stories from Guardian readers | Kayla Epstein in New York | The Guardian
evidences.content:
At this point last year, those in the US and Caribbean who found themselves in Sandys path were emerging from their homes  or what remained of them  and getting their first glimpses of the unprecedented devastation the storm left in its wake.

When we collectively think of Sandy, we instantly recall a few iconic images from the storm. But there are also other, lesser-known images that didnt make the national news, which are just as vivid today as they were a year ago for those who lived through the storm. We asked Guardian readers to tell us their memories of the Sandy they will never be able to forget, the snapshot in their mind that theyll always carry with them. Here are some of the incredible responses we received:

Patricia, 57, Larchmont, New York:"It was the first time in my life that I went to sleep at night unsure that I would be alive in the morning. The incredible relief I felt when electric crews from North Carolina and Chicago arrived almost a week later, and installed two new telephone poles and restrung our wires, so we could finally have heat, hot water, and some light. Starting a fire in the fireplace at 3pm every afternoon as the sun went around, and spending 3-4 hours in front of it to feel really warm, with cats shuffling for best position, and not having a hot shower, was starting to get old."

Ian, 61, Belvedere, New Jersey:I had been watching the track of Sandy for about a week, I had a funny feeling this would be trouble. Sure enough, it took a left turn off the Atlantic and headed right for my location. I was surprised by how little rain we were getting but later at night the wind made up for it.

I forget when the power went out but I'll never forget the roar of the wind. Laying in bed, in darkness, with no power, the roar of the wind got so much that the 200-year-old honey nut tree in my yard could take no more and came crashing into the house. It broke through the windows. There were tree branches in my bathroom with glass everywhere. It was three weeks before we got power back on. I just happened to have ordered Stieg Larsson's [Millenium] trilogy so I finished it by candlelight.

Emerick, 47, New Orleans, Louisianna: My wife and I went to [New York City] for a weekend of restaurants and museums, and had a wonderful time but failed to take into account the approaching storm. We probably didn't have time to leave anyway, and were very fortunate to manage lodging until the following weekend. It was more expensive than we had planned.

The irony of being Katrina survivors stuck in New York for a hurricane was at first depressing, but we were treated so well at every turn that we were really quite grateful for the experience. Other than being trapped in the closest pub it was pretty painless.

[Editors note: Emerick is referring to the partial collapse of the crane atop the One57 skyscraper in midtown Manhattan. You can watch a video here.]

Deborah, 32, Washington, DC: My son was born shortly before the storm arrived in the DC area. Driving to the hospital, the DC streets were eerily quiet; people had heeded the warnings and hunkered down by then. My son was born in the afternoon, and that night we heard the wind snapping branches outside the hospital window. Everyone was sending us messages saying they were glad we made it to the hospital before the storm landed. The next day my husband and I stayed at the hospital, alternating between wonderment at getting to know our first child and at the violent wind and rain pummeling the outside. For a couple of days the same nurses worked back to back shifts to attend to us, taking brief breaks to sleep in a spare room, because many roads were impassable.

Theresa, 41, Middlesex, New Jersey: Walking out of my house the morning after the storm and seeing my neighborhood. It was unreal. It was like a war zone. We were unprepared for what happened. One neighbor's shed was in another neighbor's yard, another neighbor had three massive trees on their house. Trees had come down and lifted huge chunks of sidewalk up. Fences were demolished and blown all over the neighborhood."

The other thing I won't forget is that we were all outside together, all helping each other pick up the sheds and the fences and offering cell phones that still had a charge and food and candles. We stood by each other and got to know our neighbors better after 10 years living here.

Samantha, 23, Levittown, New York:Two days after the storm, there was still no power in most homes across Long Island. But the generators at the mall were working, so I was asked to help open the store I work at. Given the already mounting gas shortage, I did not expect many families to make their way to the mall. But it was Halloween and there were still fallen power lines and split trees barricading the sidewalk."

Children were waiting in costume to trick-or-treat before we could even get the gates open. While parents searched for outlets to charge their phones, swarms of kids migrated from one store to the other, collecting candy, stickers, anything that stores had available to hand out.I heard a lot of stories throughout the day about blackouts, house damage and flooding. But despite the hardships, people were just grateful that their kids could celebrate Halloween and go trick-or-treating safely.

Albin, 37, Broad Channel, New York: When I talk about Sandy with anyone, what I most often mention is the extent to which so many of the groups of people passing through Broad Channel on their way to the Rockaway Peninsula made initial efforts to clean and move debris much more difficult than necessary. Too many times I had to tell various passersby to not be photographing through my front window as I cleaned inside, and not pick through belongings I had moved to the yard to dry and sort. While so many celebrate the wonderful spirit of "volunteerism" present in Staten Island, NJ etc, all I can do is bite my tongue to keep from cursing the pettiness that I witnessed. The city should have restricted access/passage to these groups and not allowed them into an area so debris-filled that even those of us who had to be there had little freedom of movement/vehicle access.

June, 51, Union Beach, NJ: Living through this storm in one of the hardest hit bay towns of NJ, I have learned that God is good in the midst of hardship and trauma. I saw His love through average people; people who cared enough to smile, serve, hug and weep with me. I saw such compassion in young and old; I saw the best in humanity.

Hannah, 25, London: "Sitting in my hotel room in Manhattan, I remember watching the storm beat at the windows on two sides, wondering if they were going to hold and if my family I was due to meet would have homes to return to in NJ once the evacuation was over. I doubted I would have the chance to see them at all, but when my time in New York came to an end, they insisted I still come to see them, even though they were without power and their town was in pieces. I had heard of the fabled American Spirit, and Hurricane Sandy showed me a side of it I might not have seen otherwise.
